sources.title: MySQL 8.4 Reference Manual: The Binary Log
MySQL 8.4 Reference Manual: START TRANSACTION, COMMIT, and ROLLBACK

claims.text: Redis documents cache-aside as reading Redis first, falling back to the primary on a miss, writing the fetched value back to Redis, and invalidating the cache key on updates. TTL bounds how long stale data can be served, while popular-key expiration can create a cache stampede.

Redis DEL removes keys and ignores keys that do not exist. The candidate correctly limits repeated deletion to an idempotent cache-key side effect and does not claim that DEL establishes end-to-end distributed exactly-once delivery.

MySQL 8.4 documents that binary logging happens after a statement or transaction completes but before locks are released or commit is done, and that transactional InnoDB changes are cached until COMMIT and written as the entire transaction to the binary log before COMMIT executes. COMMIT makes the transaction changes permanent. The candidate therefore keeps database durability and binlog ordering separate from whether an external cache-invalidation consumer has processed the change.

MySQL 8.4 warns not to delete old binary logs until consumers that still need them are accounted for and documents replay through mysqlbinlog. The candidate correctly treats a lost or expired CDC position as a recovery boundary that requires controlled invalidation or rebuild rather than silent continuation.

Debezium documents the outbox pattern as a way to avoid inconsistencies between a service's persisted internal state and events consumed by other services. A configured connector captures outbox-table changes and applies the outbox event router SMT; event id can be used to remove duplicates and aggregate id is used as the emitted event key for partition ordering. The candidate keeps this CDC role distinct from Redis deletion semantics.

The delayed-double-delete race explanation, hot-key singleflight or mutex or limiting controls, retry and dead-letter handling, read-your-writes bypass choices, observability metrics, and load or fault-injection plan are explicitly presented as scenario design choices or failure controls rather than undocumented Redis or MySQL defaults. They are consistent with the documented cache-aside staleness, stampede, transaction, and binary-log boundaries.

findings: The candidate directly covers delayed double-delete, binlog listening, cache-aside invalidation, stale-read windows, recoverable asynchronous invalidation, hot-key stampede, retries, observability and recovery without claiming Redis and MySQL form a single strong-consistency transaction.
Redis DEL is scoped only to repeated cache-key deletion; the answer does not turn it into an end-to-end exactly-once guarantee.
The project section is explicitly hypothetical and cannot reasonably be read as a fabricated personal production claim.
